newsitem.title: USA: American Air's Crandall says doesn't want strike.
newsitem.headline: American Air's Crandall says doesn't want strike.

text.p: American Airlines, which opened last-ditch contract talks with its pilots Monday, would lose $50 million per day as well as customers if its pilots go on strike, chairman and chief executive Robert Crandall said.
Speaking to a business group here, Crandall outlined management's position that the carrier's labor costs were already 8-9 percent higher than its leading competitors.
"If the strike occurs, we will lose $50 million in cash every day. At the end of 60 days, that rolls up to $3 billion, and at the end of 90 days, $4.5 billion," Crandall said.
"Why would we entertain a strike? The answer is we don't want to," Crandall said.

The Allied Pilots Association, representing the carrier's 9,000 pilots, began meeting in Washington with the airline's top management under a union-declared deadline of Friday at midnight for a strike.
American is a unit of AMR Corp.

Crandall said a shutdown of the airline would cost it customers too, but that its position was it had already agreed to pays its pilots the highest wages and benefits package in the industry. A deal struck previously with union negotiators was voted down by the pilots.
"They came back and asked for $200 million (more)," Crandall said of the union. "This is about money."

He also cited costs when referring to the union's rejection of a company proposal to fly smaller jets with lower-paid pilots from its commuter airlines, noting it costs 2-1/2 times as much to operate jets with the parent airline's pilots.

Other than hoping for a negotiated settlement, Crandall's solution to the impasse was mandatory binding arbitration, but he ruled out trying to operate without the pilots. "We cannot replace the pilots, we won't even try," he said.
